```
26	- **Write back to the open event** (`READ_WRITE`): add text to description, set conference data, attach the pass link / "✓ Registered" marker — but only on the *currently open* event.
27	- **Call the engine** over HTTPS via `UrlFetchApp`, attaching `getIdentityToken()` (the host's Google ID token).
28	- **Re-render** cards from action handlers (the edit/send → re-rendered card flow).
```

> AGENT

Short answer: **you cannot make the add-on pop itself open or have your backend "push" it open — Google forbids that by design — but you have two legitimate nudge paths that get you 90% of the intent.** Here's the precise breakdown, grounded in your current manifest.

## What's not possible

**1. Auto-opening the add-on's screen.** A Workspace Add-on renders only in the Calendar right rail (web) / bottom sheet (mobile), and only when the *user* taps the Auxilio icon. There is no API — for the add-on itself or for your backend — to force-expand it, grab focus, or show a badge/notification dot. This is a deliberate anti-annoyance rule. Your own limitations doc already captured it: *"No real-time / no background. Add-ons run only when the user opens an event… No push."*

**2. Your backend triggering the add-on.** The trigger relationship is strictly one-way: **Google → add-on, on a user action.** Add-on code is Google-hosted and only executes on `eventOpenTrigger` / `eventUpdateTrigger` / action handlers. The engine has no handle to invoke or render it. So "using our backend in any other way" to fire the add-on — no path exists.

## What you already have (and is the realistic answer)

**3. Contextual render on open — already wired.** Your `appsscript.json` has both `eventOpenTrigger: onCalendarEventOpen` and `eventUpdateTrigger: onCalendarEventUpdate`. So the *moment* the user opens (or saves) an event, the correct visitor card is already prepared — they just have to glance at the panel. That's as close to "auto-trigger on open/save" as the platform allows. The gap is only the one tap to open the rail.

**4. Write a nudge into the event itself — the best in-Calendar nudge.** The add-on holds `current.event.write`, and the engine's ingest path can write to events it tracks. So you can drop a passive marker that's visible the instant anyone opens the event — no add-on interaction required:
- *"⚠ External guest not registered — open Auxilio to issue a pass"* in the description, or
- *"✓ Visitor pass sent"* once done.

This is the realistic version of "nudge when the event is opened."

## If you want a true backend-initiated nudge

The backend **can** push proactively — just not *through the add-on*. Your engine already runs per-user OAuth + a Calendar watch channel (it learns about saves/changes server-side). Fire the nudge out-of-band:
- **Email / WhatsApp / Telegram** with a deep link — works even when Calendar is closed.
- **A Google Chat app** is the sanctioned in-Workspace proactive channel: a Chat app *can* post a message via API (*"3pm meeting has an external guest — register their visit?"* + button). Separate surface from the Calendar add-on, but same ecosystem, and it respects your Calendar-only/no-CASA scope line since it's its own app.

## Bottom line for the pitch

| Want | Possible? | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Add-on auto-pops open on open/save | ❌ | Google forbids it |
| Backend forces the add-on to render | ❌ | One-way trigger only |
| Right card pre-loaded the moment event opens | ✅ (have it) | `eventOpenTrigger` |
| Visible nudge inside the event on open | ✅ | write marker to event description |
| Backend-initiated nudge to the user | ✅ | engine watch → email/WhatsApp/**Chat app**, not the add-on |

So frame it as: *the add-on can't chase the user, but the event can carry a visible flag, and the engine can chase the user through a channel it already controls.* Want me to sketch the description-marker write (cheap, in the add-on you already have) or the Chat-app nudge path (new surface, more work)?

> DEVELOPER

can we not even show a notification dot?

> AGENT

No — there's no badge/dot API, and this is a hard platform limit, not a config gap.

The add-on icon in the Calendar right rail is **static** — it's just the `logoUrl` from your manifest (`appointy.svg`). CardService gives you no way to put an unread count, a red dot, or any state indicator on it. Nothing in the add-on lifecycle (`eventOpenTrigger`, `homepageTrigger`, action handlers) can touch the icon's appearance. The icon looks identical whether the open event has an unregistered external guest or nothing to do at all.

A few things people try, and why they don't work here:

- **Swap the icon to one with a dot baked in?** The `logoUrl` is resolved at manifest/deploy time and is global — you can't change it per-event or per-state. So you'd get a permanent fake "dot" that's always on, which is worse than none.
- **Toast/`Notification`?** That only fires *after* the user is already inside the add-on and triggers an action — it can't pull them in.
- **Some homepage badge?** No such surface.

So the honest hierarchy of "how loud can we be" inside Calendar:

1. **Loudest the platform allows = write into the event itself** (description marker / title prefix). This is the only thing visible *without the user opening the add-on at all* — it shows the instant they open the event. This is your de-facto "notification dot."
2. **Pre-loaded card** the moment they tap the icon (you already have this).
3. **Out-of-band** (email/WhatsApp/Chat app) if you genuinely need to *pull* the user in.

The reason this matters for the pitch: Google deliberately makes add-ons passive so they can't nag — which means **the event body is your attention surface, not the add-on chrome.** If "the guard/host must *notice* there's an unregistered visitor" is the requirement, the answer is a marker in the event plus a backend nudge, not anything on the icon.

> DEVELOPER

would it be possible if I had created a chrome extension?

> AGENT

Yes — a Chrome extension breaks through almost every wall we just hit, *because* extensions have the exact powers Google deliberately withholds from add-ons: real DOM access, a toolbar icon you control, and OS-level notifications. But it buys that power by trading directly against two of your four constraints, so it's a "yes, but read the bill" answer.

## What a Chrome extension *can* do that the add-on can't

- **Notification dot / badge — yes, real one.** `chrome.action.setBadgeText` puts a live count/dot on the extension's toolbar icon, driven by your service worker (so backend-driven). Your engine pushes → badge updates.
- **Auto-react when an event is opened or saved — yes.** A content script injected into `calendar.google.com` watches the DOM; when the event dialog opens or a save fires, you run code: pop a `chrome.sidePanel`, inject a banner *into the event dialog itself*, highlight the unregistered guest, whatever.
- **Backend-initiated push — yes.** Service worker + Web Push/FCM or polling → `chrome.notifications` (native OS toast) or badge. The backend can genuinely *chase* the user inside Calendar.
- **Overlay UI anywhere on the page** — not stuck in the right-rail card catalog. You'd escape the "card ceiling" entirely.

So everything you asked — dot, auto-open, backend nudge — is technically achievable.

## The bill (why this fights your constraints)

| Problem | Severity |
|---|---|
| **Desktop Chrome only.** No mobile Chrome, and nothing inside the Calendar *mobile app*. | 🔴 Kills it for most users |
| **Couples you to Google's obfuscated DOM.** Class names are undocumented and change without notice; your overlay breaks silently on a Google ship. | 🔴 Recurring maintenance |
| **Distribution.** Force-install needs managed-Chrome policy (Chrome Enterprise); otherwise per-user Web Store install + review. | 🟡 Setup friction |
| **Still need the engine + OAuth** for reliable event data (DOM scraping is fragile). | 🟡 Doesn't save backend work |

The first two are the real problem against **constraint #3 (mobile-first, low-end Android)** and **constraint #1 (cheap to maintain)**. Your entire reason for picking the Workspace Add-on was *"web + mobile Calendar app from one codebase, ₹0 infra, no DOM coupling."* A Chrome extension throws away the mobile half and signs you up for an indefinite "Google changed their DOM, the dot is gone" maintenance tax. And it's a **second surface**, not a replacement — you'd still keep the add-on for mobile.

## When it's actually the right call

The extension makes sense for **one narrow persona: a desktop-bound power user** — reception, an EA, an office admin who lives in Calendar web on a laptop all day and is the person who *must notice* unregistered visitors. For that user, a badge + auto-panel is genuinely good and there's no add-on equivalent.

For mobile hosts and guards — the people your four constraints are written for — it delivers nothing.

## My honest recommendation

Don't replace the add-on with an extension. If "someone must be *actively alerted*" is a real requirement, rank it this way:

1. **Event-body marker + backend nudge (email/WhatsApp/Chat app)** — works on every device, no DOM coupling. Do this first.
2. **Chrome extension** — *only* if you identify a specific desktop-bound admin persona for whom the badge is worth a permanent maintenance tax, and add it as an extra surface for that person.

If you tell me who the nudge is actually *for* (mobile host? desktop reception?), I can tell you which of these is the right spend — that's the question that decides it, not the technical feasibility.

> DEVELOPER

but how does the add on auto sync when the event page is on and the add on is open, if google does not allow us to control it from the backend?

> AGENT

Great question — it exposes the exact distinction that matters. The "auto sync" you see is **real, but it's the Google *client* firing your code, not your backend.** The direction is always one way:

```
user action in the open tab  →  Google's Calendar runtime  →  runs your add-on function  →  (your function then) calls your backend
```

Never `backend → add-on`. Let me trace what's actually happening when it "auto-syncs":

**1. You open the event** → Google's Calendar client invokes `onCalendarEventOpen(e)`. Google hands your function the event payload (attendees, title, times). Your function renders the card — and *it* may `UrlFetchApp` to your engine. The trigger was the **user opening the event**, a client-side act.

**2. You add/remove a guest and the roster updates** → that's `eventUpdateTrigger` → `onCalendarEventUpdate`. Google detected *the user changed the open event* and re-ran your function. The "live" feeling is Google re-invoking your code on a user edit — your function then re-pulls fresh data.

**3. You tap a button in the card** → your action handler runs, calls the engine, returns a new card. Again client-initiated.

In all three, the thing that "rang the doorbell" was the **user/Google client in that open tab**. Your add-on is *pulling* (via `UrlFetchApp`) in response. Your server never pushed anything — it just answered when the add-on called it.

## The proof it's client-driven, not backend-driven

Here's the tell: **sit on an open event with the add-on open, and have someone *else* change that event from another device.** Your add-on will **not** auto-refresh. No trigger fired in *your* session, so Google never re-ran your code. There's no live socket, no background poll. The add-on only "syncs" when *you* do something in that tab.

That's exactly why I said the backend can't drive it: a trigger is a doorbell only the **user + Google's client** can ring. Your backend has no wire to ring it — it can only respond when the add-on dials out.

So the two statements are consistent:
- ✅ "Auto-syncs on open/edit" → Google client → add-on (user-action triggers). This works.
- ❌ "Backend pushes the add-on / a dot / a refresh" → no such direction exists.

A Chrome extension is different *because* its service worker can hold a push connection (FCM/Web Push) and update the badge with no user action — that's the capability the add-on structurally lacks.

> DEVELOPER

can we not auto open the add on when the calendar event opens?

> AGENT

No — there's genuinely no "open my panel" API. Not for the add-on, not for the backend, not even on the user's own event-open action. I want to be definitive because you've circled this a few times: **Google does not expose a way to force the side panel from closed → open.** That's a deliberate platform decision, not a missing setting.

But there's one real nuance that probably explains why it sometimes *feels* like it auto-opens, and it's useful:

## The panel's open/closed state is sticky across the session

The add-on side panel has a **persistent open/closed state** within a Calendar session. So:

- If the panel is **closed** and you open an event → `eventOpenTrigger` runs your code (prepares the card), but the panel stays closed. User sees nothing until they click the Auxilio icon.
- If the panel is **already open** and you move to / open another event → your contextual card **auto-renders in the already-open panel**, no click needed.

So once the user opens Auxilio *once*, it "follows them" — every event they open after that auto-populates the panel. That sticky behavior is the closest thing to auto-open, and it's free with the `eventOpenTrigger` you already have. What you cannot do is the initial closed → open jump.

## What this means practically

You can't engineer "panel pops open on event open." What you *can* do:

1. **Lean on stickiness** — get the user to open Auxilio once at the start of their session (onboarding nudge: "pin Auxilio"), and it stays open and auto-renders per event for the rest of the session.
2. **Put the attention-grab in the event body**, not the panel — the description marker, which is visible whether the panel is open or not. Still the only thing you control that shows without any tap.

So the wall is real and final: **no force-open.** The lever you have is the panel's own stickiness plus a marker in the event. If forcing the UI open is a hard requirement for the pitch, that's the line that pushes you toward a Chrome extension (desktop-only) — there's no add-on path to it.

> DEVELOPER

how to give the onboarding nudge?

> AGENT

"Onboarding nudge" splits into two different jobs, and only one of them lives in your code. Let me be concrete about each, because the add-on still can't promote itself — the nudge has to come from outside it or be baked into the event.

## Job 1 — Discovery: get them to open Auxilio the *first* time

The add-on can't announce itself, so this is a one-time, mostly-human push. Cheapest first (the Ameya lens):

1. **Admin rollout message (₹0, do this regardless).** You're internal-first with admin one-click domain push — so pair the push with a one-time announcement over a channel you already use (email / WhatsApp / company Chat): *"Auxilio now lives in your Google Calendar. Open any event and look for the purple Appointy icon on the right to register a visitor."* One screenshot, done. This is the real onboarding; no tech.

2. **Event-body pointer (engine-side, proactive).** When the engine's ingest detects an external guest on an event, have it patch a line into the event description: *"👉 Open Auxilio in the sidebar to send this visitor a pass."* This shows the moment they open the event, pointing at the icon. **Note the constraint:** this has to be written by the **engine** (its broad-OAuth ingest path), not the add-on — the add-on can only write the *currently-open* event, so it can't pre-place the marker before they've opened it.

3. **Backend nudge (optional, pulls them in).** The engine already runs a Calendar watch, so on "external guest added" it can fire a message with a deep link / how-to. Same mechanism as the general nudge we discussed — works on mobile too.

## Job 2 — Stickiness education: "keep it open, it'll follow you"

This one *is* in your code, and it's the cheap win. The first time someone opens the add-on, show a one-time card section, gated by a flag so it never nags again:

```js
function maybePrependOnboarding(card, e) {
  const props = PropertiesService.getUserProperties();
  if (props.getProperty('auxilio_onboarded')) return card;
  // prepend a section: "Tip: keep Auxilio open — it follows you to every event you open."
  // + a "Got it" TextButton → onDismissOnboarding
}

function onDismissOnboarding(e) {
  PropertiesService.getUserProperties().setProperty('auxilio_onboarded', '1');
  // re-render the normal card
}
```

Drop the `maybePrependOnboarding` call into your existing `onCalendarEventOpen` / `onHomepage` render path. `PropertiesService` is per-user, free, Google-hosted — no infra.

## One honesty caveat — don't promise a permanent "pin"

There's no programmatic "pin Auxilio forever" you can set. The panel's open state is **per-session** (and cross-session persistence is Google's behavior, not something you control or can rely on). So realistically: you educate them once (Job 2), and accept they may need to click the icon once per session. You can't detect whether the panel is currently open either, so you can't conditionally re-nudge based on panel state — only on event state (external guest present) and the first-run flag.

## My recommendation

Do **#1 (admin announcement)** + **the in-add-on first-run card (Job 2)** now — both are ₹0 and cover 80% of discovery and the stickiness concept. Add **#2 (engine event-body pointer)** when you wire the external-guest detection, since it's the most in-context reminder and reuses the ingest write path.

but if the add on panel can refresh and update programatically, how can we not trigger it when any calendaar event happens, can it not open up on calendar evetns?

> AGENT

You've found the exact seam, so let me name it precisely, because it resolves the contradiction:

**Updating the card and opening the panel are two different capabilities. The API gives you the first and deliberately withholds the second.**

Here's the mechanism that makes "programmatic refresh" *feel* like it should be able to open the panel, but doesn't:

When a calendar event opens, your `onCalendarEventOpen` runs and **returns a Card**. That's it — your function's only job is to *hand Google a card*. It does **not** issue a "show yourself" command. Google's runtime then decides what to do with that card:

- Panel already open → it paints your new card. (This is the "auto-refresh" you've seen.)
- Panel closed → it **holds** the card and paints it only when the user opens the panel.

So the "programmatic update" is **a return value, not an outbound action.** You're not pushing to the UI — you're answering an invocation with content, and Google owns whether/when that content becomes visible. Look at the whole navigation API: `Navigation.pushCard`, `updateCard`, `popCard` — every one of them rearranges cards *inside an already-open panel*. **There is no method anywhere that means "panel: become visible."** Not `openPanel()`, nothing. The closed→open transition is simply not in the surface area Google exposes to add-on code.

An analogy that fits exactly:

> It's a **billboard the city repaints whenever you walk past it** (you walking past = `eventOpenTrigger`; the city = Google's runtime). You control *what gets painted*. You cannot make the billboard *get up and move in front of someone's face*. The repaint is programmatic; the placement is the city's, not yours.

And the reason Google built it this way is intentional: if any add-on could force its panel open on every event, Calendar would be a brawl of add-ons fighting for the screen on every click. So Google reserved "panel visibility" as a **user-only** decision. Your code provides content; the user provides attention.

So, directly: **no, it cannot open up on calendar events.** The `eventOpenTrigger` firing gives you a hook to *prepare/update content*, never to *summon the surface*. The only time content auto-appears is when the user has already opened the panel — then it's already "on," so your updates show.

That separation — **content-provider yes, surface-controller no** — is the whole wall in one sentence. A Chrome extension is the opposite: it *is* a surface-controller (it can open a side panel, inject DOM, set a badge), which is precisely why it's the only path to "force it open," and precisely why it costs you mobile + ongoing DOM maintenance.

> DEVELOPER

but suppose a 1000 people use it via chromse extension, and I am assuming we will be connected to the chrome extensions via sse or socket , would not it overload our server?

> AGENT

Two answers here: the direct one (no, 1000 won't overload you), and a more important correction (on a Chrome extension you shouldn't be holding sockets at all). The second one is the one that matters.

## Direct answer: 1000 connections is trivially small

The instinct that "1000 sockets = overload" is almost always wrong at this scale. **Idle connections are cheap** — the cost is mostly a file descriptor + some socket buffers, on the order of tens of KB each:

- 1000 idle SSE/WebSocket ≈ **~30–80 MB RAM, ~0% CPU** while idle. A single small instance handles it without noticing.
- A tuned Node/Bun/Go process holds **tens of thousands** of idle connections fine. The "C10k problem" (10,000 concurrent) was solved ~20 years ago. 1000 is 1% of that.

What actually loads a server is **not connection count — it's messages/sec × work-per-message.** A held connection that delivers ~3 nudges a day costs you almost nothing. So the fear is misdirected: connection *count* is cheap; *event throughput and the DB work each event triggers* is what you'd engineer around, and your nudge volume is tiny (a handful of external-guest events per user per day).

## The real correction: don't hold sockets from the extension at all

Your premise — *"connected via SSE or socket"* — is the part I'd push back on, because of how Chrome extensions actually work now:

**Manifest V3 extensions can't reliably hold a persistent connection.** The background page is gone; it's a **non-persistent service worker** that Chrome **kills after ~30 seconds idle**. Your SSE/socket would get torn down constantly and you'd fight reconnection storms — which, ironically, is the one thing that *could* load your server (1000 clients reconnecting in a loop). So the held-socket model is the wrong tool here, independent of scale.

The sanctioned pattern is **Web Push / FCM**:

```
Google Calendar watch → your engine (already receives the change)
        → POST to FCM  → Chrome's push service → wakes the extension service worker → badge/notification
```

With this, **your server holds zero persistent connections.** You already receive calendar changes via the watch channel you run in the engine; you just hand the last hop to FCM. Google fans it out to all 1000 clients. FCM is **free**. Your server's job shrinks to "POST a small message when a real state change happens" — fully stateless, scales to 1000 or 100,000 the same way.

## So, the honest scaling picture

| Approach | Server holds 1000 conns? | MV3-viable? | Cost at 1000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| SSE/WebSocket held open | Yes (but cheap) | ❌ killed at 30s idle | low runtime, **high fragility** |
| **Web Push / FCM** | **No — zero** | ✅ the intended model | **~₹0, stateless** |
| Poll on Calendar focus | No | ✅ | ₹0, cruder/laggier |

**Recommendation:** if you go the extension route, use **FCM**, not sockets. It removes the scaling question entirely — you're never holding connections, so "1000 users" never becomes a server-sizing problem. The cost that does scale with an extension isn't runtime at all; it's the **engineering + DOM-maintenance tax** I flagged earlier and the **desktop-only** limitation — those are the real bill, not connection count.

One more honest note for the pitch: none of this — FCM, sockets, badges — works inside the **Calendar mobile app**, which is where most of your hosts live. So even with a perfectly scaled extension, you're solving the nudge for desktop users only. That trade, not server load, is the decision.

> DEVELOPER

can a workspace admin install a chrome extension for every account in the workspace?

> AGENT

Yes — a Workspace admin can force-install a Chrome extension to the whole org, silently, no per-user action. But the *reach* of that install is narrower than it sounds, and that's the part that matters for your decision.

## The mechanism (yes, it works)

**Admin console → Devices → Chrome → Apps & extensions → Users & browsers → set the extension to "Force install."** Scope it to an OU or the whole domain. Result:

- Installs automatically, silently, on next Chrome sync. User can't remove it.
- Works with a **private/unlisted** extension — publish it to the Chrome Web Store restricted to your domain (or self-host the `.crx`) and force-install **by extension ID**. No public listing needed — same "internal-first" posture as your add-on.

So distribution parity with the add-on is real: admin pushes once, everyone gets it.

## The conditions (where "every account" gets narrower)

The policy binds to **managed Chrome**, not to the Google account in the abstract. A user actually receives it only when:

- They're signed into **Chrome (desktop) with their managed Workspace account** — user-level cloud policy follows the signed-in profile, so **no device enrollment is required** for Workspace-managed users; or
- They're on an enrolled/managed browser or ChromeOS device.

What that excludes:

- **Mobile entirely.** Chrome on Android/iOS doesn't run extensions. None of your phone-based hosts get it. (This is the same wall as before, now showing up at the distribution layer.)
- **Other browsers / not signed into Chrome.** Someone on Safari, Firefox, or a Chrome profile without the corp account dodges it. So it's "force-installed for everyone *using managed desktop Chrome*," not literally every human.

## How this compares to the add-on push

| | Workspace Add-on | Chrome extension (force-install) |
|---|---|---|
| Admin one-click to whole org | ✅ | ✅ |
| Silent, no user action | ✅ | ✅ |
| Private/internal-only | ✅ | ✅ (unlisted by ID) |
| **Reaches Calendar *mobile app*** | ✅ | ❌ |
| **Reaches desktop web** | ✅ | ✅ |
| Couples to Google's DOM (maintenance) | ❌ | 🔴 yes |

So the honest read for the pitch: **distribution is not the differentiator** — admin can blanket-push either one. The differentiator is unchanged: the add-on reaches **web + the Calendar mobile app** with zero DOM maintenance; the extension reaches **desktop Chrome only** and adds the can-force-open / badge / push powers at the cost of mobile and a permanent maintenance tax. If your nudge target is desktop reception/EA staff, force-install is a clean way to guarantee they all have it. If it's mobile hosts, force-install doesn't help — they're not in scope of any extension.

> AGENT

Let me give you the straight analysis, because there's a genuinely good idea buried here (the magic address) and one structural limit that won't go away no matter how well you build it.

## Verdict up front

**On desktop Chrome: yes — the extension can do everything the add-on does and meaningfully better, and your magic-address trigger is the right instinct.** But two things stay true no matter how good the build is:

1. **It's desktop-only.** It cannot run where the add-on's mobile half runs (the Calendar mobile app). So it doesn't *replace* the add-on — it's a richer **second surface**, and the two should be unified by the magic address, not chosen between.
2. **It carries a permanent DOM-maintenance tax** that the add-on doesn't.

So the honest framing isn't "extension vs. add-on." It's "**one signal (the magic address), multiple reactors**" — which actually matches your own architecture rule (channel-agnostic core, dumb adapters).

## Feature-by-feature: can the extension deliver the vision?

| Vision item | Extension on desktop Chrome | vs. add-on |
|---|---|---|
| Realtime guest updates as you edit | ✅ `MutationObserver` on the event editor → instant panel update, no round-trip | **Better** (add-on re-renders a whole card server-side via `eventUpdateTrigger`) |
| Per-guest invite toggle | ✅ real React state, instant | **Better** (no card rebuild per toggle) |
| Email template preview + select | ✅ full HTML/CSS — real preview | **Much better** — this is exactly the "card ceiling" your own limitations doc flagged |
| Edit user data inline | ✅ smooth multi-field forms | **Better** (CardService form state is "fragile," per your doc) |
| Auto-update / realtime / state mgmt | ✅ its home turf | **Better** |
| Auto-nudge when event is saved | ✅ detect save (DOM/network) → nudge | add-on can't nudge, only pre-render |
| OAuth | ✅ (see design note below) | parity |

So every UX item you listed is achievable, and the ones that strain the add-on (template preview, inline edit, smooth toggles) are precisely where the extension shines. The "card ceiling" your team documented as the risk to the D5 bet simply doesn't exist in an extension.

## The one technical gotcha on "auto-open"

You should know this before you pitch it as easy: **`chrome.sidePanel.open()` requires a user gesture** in Manifest V3 — you can't open the official side panel purely because your code detected something. Two clean ways around it:

- **Inject your own panel into the page DOM** (a content-script overlay). No gesture required, so it *can* auto-appear on detecting the magic address. Cost: this is *more* DOM coupling (deeper maintenance tax).
- **Use the "mark as visitor" affordance as the gesture** (see below) — the user's click legitimately opens the side panel *and* does the marking.

Both work. The first gives you true "pops open by itself"; the second is cleaner and less fragile. You'll likely use the injected-DOM approach for the auto-surface-on-reopen case and the gesture for first-time marking.

## The magic address — yes, it's good UX, and it's smarter than you may realize

Your instinct to make the nudge **intentional rather than fire on every event** is correct, and the magic address is the right primitive for three reasons:

**1. It converts "auto-open" from annoying to expected.** Blanket auto-open on every event = the exact nagging Google designed add-ons to prevent. But gated on a marker *the user themselves added*, the panel only surfaces for events they opted into. The user is never surprised — they marked it, so they expect it. That distinction is the whole reason this is good UX rather than bad.

**2. You already have this primitive.** Your engine's calendar→visitor pipeline already uses a magic-address ingest path. So reusing it as the extension's trigger isn't a new concept — it's the **same "this is a visitor event" signal**, now read by one more reactor. That's the cleanest possible fit with "domains are plugin-shaped, channels are dumb adapters."

**3. It decouples intent from surface.** The intent lives as *data in the event*, not as a UI gesture on one platform. So the same marked event is recognized by: the extension (desktop, auto-surfaces rich UI), the add-on (mobile, renders its card), and the engine's watch (server-side, can nudge via WhatsApp/Chat/email). One mark, every surface reacts appropriately. **This is what actually completes your vision across devices** — not the extension alone.

### The refinement that makes it work: don't make anyone type a magic string

The risk with a magic address is discoverability + literacy (constraint #2) — a host won't remember `visitor@…` or a magic location. So **never make them type it.** Give them an affordance that does both jobs at once:

> The extension injects a one-click **"Register a visitor for this event"** button into the event UI. Clicking it (a) is a user gesture → legitimately opens the panel, and (b) stamps the event with the magic address (as a guest/resource/location) so the engine and the mobile add-on also see it on save.

That single click = *open the rich UI now* **+** *persist the cross-surface signal*. It also neatly dodges the `sidePanel.open()` gesture requirement. Then on **re-opening** an already-marked event, the extension detects the magic address and auto-surfaces the injected panel (dismissible — keep it forgiving, constraint #2). First-time = intentional click; thereafter = auto-context. That's a genuinely better flow than the add-on's "tap the icon every time."

(You could also register the magic address as a saved Contact named "Add Visitor" so it shows in the guest autocomplete — a second discoverable on-ramp. Belt and suspenders.)

## The honest costs — what to put in front of leadership (and Ameya)

1. **Mobile gap is the real decision, not server load or features.** Ask the concrete question: *where do your hosts actually register visitors?* If they're office employees at desks in Calendar web, desktop-only is largely fine and the extension is strong value. If a meaningful share register from their phones, the extension can't serve them — and you keep the add-on for them. Either way, **the add-on doesn't go away**; the extension is additive.

2. **Two surfaces = double maintenance**, and the extension's share includes a **DOM-coupling tax**: Google ships Calendar UI changes with no notice, and your event-open detection, save detection, magic-address detection, and injected panel all sit on top of that un-documented DOM. Budget for "it broke after a Google update" as a recurring line item. This is the cost that scales with *time*, not users — and it's the one that hits Ameya's "cost aayega."

3. **OAuth — keep the engine as the single token holder.** Don't give the extension its own broad Calendar OAuth if you can avoid it. Cleanest design consistent with your "dumb adapter" rule: the extension authenticates the user for **identity only**, reads the in-progress event from the **page DOM** (for live editing immediacy), and calls the **engine** for authoritative data, template lists, dedup, and send. The engine already holds the Calendar OAuth + watch. That keeps tokens in one place and the extension thin. Internal-first (force-installed, unlisted) keeps you **exempt from Google OAuth verification**, same posture as the add-on. Stay Calendar-only — never add Gmail/Drive — to avoid CASA, exactly as your add-on rules already state.

4. **Async delivery = FCM, not held sockets** (from our last exchange): the engine pushes nudges via FCM, so 1,000 users is a non-event for your server.

## My recommendation

**Don't position this as replacing the add-on. Position the magic address as the unifying signal and the extension as the desktop power-surface over it:**

- **Magic address** = the one intentional "this is a visitor event" marker (you already have it).
- **Desktop** → extension: rich UI, auto-surface on marked events, the better UX you're describing.
- **Mobile** → add-on stays: card flow, keyed off the same magic address.
- **Offline/async** → engine watch → FCM/WhatsApp/Chat nudge.

On **sequencing**, apply your own team's logic: your add-on doc says *defer the richer web surface (D6) until the card ceiling is proven painful in practice.* The extension is essentially that richer surface, in-page. So I'd **spike it** — build the magic-address detect + one-click-mark + auto-surface + template-preview as a focused desktop prototype for the host persona — and validate two things before committing to maintaining it forever: (a) that hosts really are on desktop, and (b) that the UX win over the add-on card is big enough to justify the DOM tax. If both hold, the extension becomes the primary desktop surface and the add-on the mobile fallback. If hosts turn out to be mobile-heavy, you've spent a spike, not a second product.

Net: **your vision is achievable and your magic-address idea is the best part of it** — it's the thing that makes the auto-open *good* UX instead of nagging, and it's the thing that ties desktop, mobile, and backend into one coherent system. Just go in clear-eyed that the extension buys you superior desktop UX in exchange for desktop-only reach and a standing maintenance cost — and that the magic address, not the extension, is what actually unifies the whole vision.

> DEVELOPER

how those AI chat extension open chrome side panels, can we not do that?

> AGENT

Good question to chase down, because it exposes a subtlety: those AI extensions open the side panel **the same three ways**, and every one of them is **user-initiated**. None of them pops the official side panel open on its own from a page event. Here's exactly how they do it:

## How Sider / Monica / ChatGPT-sidebar actually open the panel

There are only a few sanctioned triggers for `chrome.sidePanel`, and they all require user action:

1. **Toolbar icon click** — the most common. They call once at startup:
   ```js
   chrome.sidePanel.setPanelBehavior({ openPanelOnActionClick: true });
   ```
   Now clicking the extension's icon opens the panel. Chrome handles the gesture; you don't even call `open()`.

2. **Keyboard shortcut** — they register a command (`chrome.commands`), and the keypress handler calls `chrome.sidePanel.open()`. The keypress *is* the user gesture, so it's allowed.

3. **Right-click context menu** — "Open sidebar" menu item; the menu click is the gesture → `open()`.

`chrome.sidePanel.open()` itself **must be called in response to a user gesture** — that's the rule, and it hasn't changed. Those three are just the three legal gesture sources.

## The thing to notice

Those AI extensions feel "always there," but they **do not auto-open the official side panel from a page event** — you click the icon, hit the hotkey, or pick the menu. They can't summon the Chrome side panel purely because something happened on the page, *for the exact same reason the add-on can't* — Chrome reserves panel-opening as a user decision. So "can we not do what they do?" — yes, we can do **everything** they do (icon/hotkey/context-menu open). But that's still user-initiated, which is precisely *not* the "auto-open when the magic-address event loads, no click" behavior you're after.

## So how do you get the auto-feel?

Two honest options, and they trade robustness against magic:

**Option A — official side panel, one click (robust).** When your content script detects the magic address, it **auto-injects a small dismissible banner into the event page** (DOM injection needs *no* gesture). The banner says *"Visitor event — open Auxilio."* The user's one click on it is the gesture that opens the real side panel. So: detection is automatic; the panel open is one click. You get Chrome's clean panel UI and stay off the fragile path.

**Option B — injected DOM overlay, zero click (fully auto, more fragile).** Skip `chrome.sidePanel` entirely and render your whole panel as a content-script overlay on the page. That *can* appear with no user action the instant the magic address is detected — true auto-open. Cost: it's your own DOM injected into Calendar, so it deepens the maintenance tax we discussed, and it's not the native side panel.

One caveat so you don't get surprised in the build: the *"inject a floating button in the page → click it → service worker calls `sidePanel.open()`"* path (forwarding the gesture from content script to the worker) has been **finicky and version-dependent**. The reliable gesture sources remain the toolbar icon, a `chrome.commands` hotkey, and a context-menu click. So if you want guaranteed behavior, lean on those for the official panel (Option A's banner can itself be wired to trigger the action), and use Option B's overlay when you truly want no-click auto-appearance.

**Net:** the AI extensions aren't doing anything you can't — but they're also **not** auto-opening the native panel from page events; they wait for you to click/hotkey. Real auto-open with zero user action only exists via **injected DOM** (Option B), at the price of more coupling. The magic-address-detection → **auto-injected banner → one-click opens the native panel** (Option A) is the sweet spot: it feels automatic, keeps the native side panel, and avoids the fragile bits.

> DEVELOPER

okay, Do A, but will this extension be approved if we go commerical/public?

> AGENT

Quick flag before the answer: "Do A" locks the *design* (auto-injected banner → one-click opens the native side panel) — good, that's the right pick. But there's no extension codebase yet, and your "but will it be approved" is a gating question you clearly want resolved *before* committing build effort. So let me answer that properly; I'm not going to start coding an extension while the go/no-go is still open. Here's the honest approval picture.

## You face two separate gates, not one

For a public/commercial extension that touches Google Calendar, "approval" is actually **two independent reviews**, and people forget the second one:

| Gate | What it reviews | Trigger | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Chrome Web Store review** | The extension package: permissions, single-purpose, privacy policy, no remote code | Publishing publicly | Free, usually days |
| **Google OAuth verification** | Your OAuth *consent screen* + scope usage | Using a **sensitive** scope (Calendar) with users outside your org | Free, days–weeks |

While you're **internal-first** (force-installed, unlisted, your Workspace domain only) you're exempt from *both* public-facing reviews. The moment you go **public/commercial to other orgs**, both kick in. That's the real cost of "going public" — not money, but two verification hoops and ongoing compliance.

## Will it be approved? Realistically — yes, this class of extension is approvable

There's no policy that blocks injecting a sidebar into Calendar or using Calendar OAuth. Public Calendar-enhancing extensions with OAuth already exist. You get approved if you hold these lines:

**Chrome Web Store side:**
- **Narrow host permissions.** Request `https://calendar.google.com/*` only — *not* `<all_urls>`. Broad host permissions are the #1 thing that draws scrutiny/rejection. Single-host is easily justified.
- **Single, clear purpose.** "Register office visitors from a Calendar event." Clean.
- **No remotely-hosted code (MV3 hard rule).** Bundle all your JS. You may fetch **data (JSON)** from your engine, but never executable code/scripts. This is a common rejection cause — make sure your build bundles everything.
- **Privacy policy + data disclosure.** You read attendee data (personal data), so you must disclose what you collect and comply with **Google's Limited Use** requirements for user data (same regime as your add-on).
- **Non-deceptive branding.** "Auxilio Visitor for Google Calendar" is fine if you follow Google's "for Google Calendar" attribution rules and don't imply you *are* Google.

**OAuth verification side:**
- **Stay Calendar-only.** Calendar is a *sensitive* scope → verification, but **no CASA**. The instant you add Gmail or Drive, it becomes *restricted* → annual paid **CASA security assessment**. You've already designed your add-on around this exact line — hold it for the extension too.
- You'll need: a published privacy policy, a homepage, scope justifications, and a **demo video** of the OAuth flow. Routine, just takes time.

None of these are blockers. They're hoops. The things that actually get you **rejected**: broad/unjustified permissions, remote code, missing/weak privacy policy, or deceptive Google-branding.

## Two commercial-specific things you may not be expecting

1. **You can't charge *through* the Chrome Web Store.** Google shut down CWS payments/licensing years ago. So "commercial" means the extension is free to install and **you bill via your own backend** (account/license/subscription on your engine). Common and fine — just know the store isn't your payment rail.

2. **Keep OAuth in the engine, not the extension — it also simplifies verification.** If the *extension* requests its own Google OAuth (`chrome.identity`), then the extension's OAuth client needs verification. If instead the **engine** holds the Calendar OAuth (web flow) and the extension just authenticates the user to the engine + reads the live DOM, you have **one OAuth app to verify** (the engine's) serving add-on, extension, and ingest alike. For a multi-tenant commercial product that's cleaner legally and for review. This is the same thin-adapter placement I recommended earlier — it pays off again here.

## The honest risk flags for going commercial

- **You're now a data processor for other businesses' calendar data.** Public/commercial multi-tenant = DPAs, GDPR posture, data-handling commitments. That's a **business/legal** layer beyond store approval — bigger than the technical review, and worth raising with leadership explicitly.
- **Double platform dependency.** You're subject to CWS policy *and* OAuth verification *and* your DOM coupling to Calendar. Three Google-controlled surfaces that can shift under you. For a commercial product, that's concentration risk to name in the pitch.
- **Re-review on changes.** Each scope addition re-triggers OAuth verification; each update gets a (usually fast) CWS re-review. Adding a restricted scope later = CASA. Budget the Calendar-only discipline as a permanent constraint, not a one-time choice.

## Bottom line

**Approvable, yes — provided you stay Calendar-only (no CASA), keep host permissions to `calendar.google.com`, bundle all code (no remote JS), ship a real privacy policy with Limited Use compliance, and pass OAuth verification.** The blockers are all self-inflicted (broad permissions, remote code, weak privacy disclosure); the real costs are *time* (verification) and the *legal/data-processor* layer that commercial multi-tenant brings — not money to Google, since the store no longer takes payments.

My recommendation on sequencing, given approval is your concern: **ship it internal-first** (your Workspace, force-installed, unlisted — zero verification) to prove the UX and the magic-address flow with real hosts. Going public is then a *packaging + verification* exercise over code that already works — the same staged path your add-on already follows. Don't pay the verification/legal cost until the internal version has earned it.

```json
  "content": "# Calendar Visitor — Chrome Extension Surface (Decision Doc)\n\n**Date:** 2026-06-18\n**Status:** Decision locked on UX approach (Option A) + sequencing; build not started.\n**Read alongside:**\n- `../auxilio-workspace/docs/2026-06-17_workspace_addon_possibilities_and_limitations.md` (why the add-on hits a ceiling)\n- `../auxilio-workspace/CLAUDE.md` (scope rules, internal-first, Calendar-only/no-CASA line)\n- `2026-06-16_calendar_visitor_addon_build_plan.md` (the add-on plan this complements)\n- `../office-ops-engine/spec/2026-06-16_calendar_addon_register_endpoint.md` (the engine contract both surfaces share)\n\n---\n\n## TL;DR\n\nA Chrome extension can deliver the full host flow (realtime guest updates, per-guest invite toggle, template preview/select, inline edits) **with better UX than the add-on — on desktop Chrome only.** It is **not a replacement** for the add-on; it is a richer **second surface**. The two are unified by one primitive: the **magic address** that marks an event as a visitor event.\n\n- **Locked UX = Option A:** detect the magic address → auto-inject a dismissible in-page banner (no gesture needed) → one click opens the **native Chrome side panel** with the rich UI. This avoids the fragile auto-open paths while still feeling automatic.\n- **OAuth stays in the engine.** The extension authenticates the user for identity and calls the engine; the engine holds the Calendar OAuth + watch. One OAuth app to verify, thin-adapter extension.\n- **Internal-first, then public.** Force-install to our Workspace (unlisted, zero verification) to prove the flow. Going public is a packaging + verification exercise later — don't pay that cost until the internal version earns it.\n\n---\n\n## Why a second surface at all\n\nThe add-on is correct for **mobile + low-friction**, but CardService has a hard ceiling (documented in the add-on limitations doc): no free-form UI, every interaction is a server round-trip that rebuilds a card, fragile form state, limited rich text. Template preview, multi-guest inline edits, and smooth toggles all strain it. A Chrome extension has the powers the add-on structurally lacks: real DOM, full HTML/CSS/JS UI, client-side state, a toolbar badge, and OS/Web-Push notifications.\n\n### What each surface can and can't do\n\n| Capability | Workspace Add-on | Chrome Extension (desktop) |\n|---|---|---|\n| Runs on Calendar **mobile app** | ✅ | ❌ (extensions are desktop Chrome only) |\n| Runs on Calendar **web** | ✅ | ✅ |\n| Rich UI (template preview, inline edit, smooth toggles) | ❌ card ceiling | ✅ full React UI |\n| Realtime guest updates as you edit | re-renders a card server-side | ✅ `MutationObserver`, instant |\n| Auto-open / auto-surface | ❌ never (Google forbids) | ✅ via injected DOM (Option A/B) |\n| Badge / notification dot | ❌ | ✅ |\n| Backend-initiated nudge | ❌ (one-way trigger) | ✅ via FCM/Web Push |\n| Couples to Google's obfuscated DOM | ❌ none | 🔴 yes — recurring maintenance tax |\n| Admin one-click install to whole org | ✅ | ✅ (Chrome force-install policy) |\n\n**The two unchanging truths:** the extension is **desktop-only** (cannot serve hosts on the Calendar mobile app), and it carries a **permanent DOM-maintenance tax** (Google ships Calendar UI changes without notice). These are the real costs — not features, not server load.\n\n---\n\n## The magic address is the unifying primitive\n\nThe intentional-trigger instinct is correct: **do not nudge on every calendar event** (that's the nagging Google designed add-ons to prevent). Instead, an event becomes a \"visitor event\" only when it carries the **magic address** — a marker the host opts into.\n\nWhy this is the right design:\n\n1. **Converts auto-open from annoying → expected.** The panel only surfaces for events the user themselves marked. Never a surprise.\n2. **Reuses an existing concept.** The engine's calendar→visitor pipeline already keys off a magic address. This is the *same* \"this is a visitor event\" signal, read by one more reactor.\n3. **Decouples intent from surface.** Intent lives as **data in the event**, not a UI gesture on one platform. The same marked event is recognized by the extension (desktop), the add-on (mobile), and the engine's watch (server-side, can nudge via WhatsApp/Chat/email).\n\n### Don't make anyone type a magic string\n\nDiscoverability + literacy (constraint #2) means the host must never type/remember the address. Provide an affordance:\n\n- The extension injects a **\"Register a visitor for this event\"** button. Clicking it (a) is a user gesture → legitimately opens the side panel, and (b) **stamps the event with the magic address** so the engine and mobile add-on also see it on save.\n- Optionally register the magic address as a saved **Contact** (\"Add Visitor\") so it appears in the guest autocomplete — a second on-ramp.\n\nSo **one click = open rich UI now + persist the cross-surface signal.** First-time = intentional click; on re-opening an already-marked event, the extension detects the magic address and auto-surfaces (Option A).\n\n---\n\n## Locked UX: Option A (auto-banner → one-click native side panel)\n\nWhy not just auto-open the side panel? `chrome.sidePanel.open()` **requires a user gesture** (MV3). The reliable gesture sources are the toolbar icon (`setPanelBehavior({openPanelOnActionClick:true})`), a `chrome.commands` hotkey, and a context-menu click. Even the AI-chat sidebar extensions (Sider/Monica/ChatGPT) open this way — none auto-open the native panel from a page event.\n\n**Option A (chosen):**\n1. Content script detects the magic address on the open event (DOM injection needs **no** gesture).\n2. Auto-injects a small, **dismissible** banner into the event UI: *\"Visitor event — open Auxilio.\"*\n3. The user's **one click** on the banner is the gesture → opens the **native Chrome side panel** with the full React UI.\n\nThis feels automatic, keeps the clean native panel, and stays off the finicky content-script→service-worker gesture-forwarding path.\n\n**Option B (rejected for now):** render the whole panel as an injected DOM overlay → truly zero-click auto-open, but deeper DOM coupling and not the native panel. Revisit only if one-click proves to be friction.\n\nKeep the banner dismissible and the panel non-trapping (constraint #2, forgiving).\n\n---\n\n## OAuth placement: engine holds it, extension is a thin client\n\n- Extension authenticates the **user's identity** (sign-in to the engine), reads the in-progress event from the **page DOM** for live-editing immediacy, and calls the **engine** for authoritative data, template list, dedup, and send.\n- The **engine** holds the broad Calendar OAuth + watch (already does, for ingest).\n- Result: **one OAuth app to verify** (the engine's) serving add-on, extension, and ingest alike — cleaner for verification and for keeping the extension a \"dumb adapter\" per the umbrella architecture.\n\n**Async nudges = FCM/Web Push**, never held sockets. MV3 service workers can't hold a persistent connection (killed ~30s idle), and held sockets would invite reconnection storms. With FCM the server holds **zero** connections; 1,000+ users is a non-event. The engine already receives calendar changes via its watch channel — it just hands the last hop to FCM.\n\n---\n\n## Will it be approved if we go commercial/public?\n\n**Yes — this class of extension is approvable**, provided we hold specific lines. Public + Calendar = **two independent gates**:\n\n| Gate | Reviews | Trigger | Cost |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| **Chrome Web Store review** | package, permissions, single-purpose, privacy policy, no remote code | publishing publicly | free, ~days |\n| **Google OAuth verification** | OAuth consent screen + scope justification | sensitive (Calendar) scope for users outside our org | free, ~days–weeks |\n\nWhile **internal-first** (force-installed, unlisted, our domain), we are **exempt from both**. Going public/commercial to other orgs triggers both.\n\n### What gets us approved\n- **Narrow host permissions:** `https://calendar.google.com/*` only — never `<all_urls>` (the #1 scrutiny/rejection cause).\n- **No remotely-hosted code (MV3 hard rule):** bundle all JS; fetch only **data (JSON)** from the engine, never executable code.\n- **Single clear purpose:** \"register office visitors from a Calendar event.\"\n- **Privacy policy + data disclosure + Google Limited Use** compliance (we read attendee = personal data).\n- **Non-deceptive branding:** \"Auxilio Visitor for Google Calendar,\" following Google's attribution/brand rules — don't imply we are Google.\n- **Stay Calendar-only:** Calendar is *sensitive* → verification but **no CASA**. Gmail/Drive are *restricted* → annual paid **CASA security assessment**. Hold this line (same as the add-on rule).\n\n### What gets us rejected\nBroad/unjustified permissions, remote code, missing/weak privacy policy, deceptive Google branding. All self-inflicted and avoidable.\n\n### Commercial specifics\n- **Can't charge through the Web Store** — Google shut down CWS payments. The extension installs free; **bill via our own engine** (account/license/subscription).\n- **We become a data processor for other orgs' calendar data** → DPAs, GDPR posture, data-handling commitments. This **business/legal layer is bigger than the store review** — raise it explicitly with leadership.\n\n### Standing risks to name in the pitch\n- **Double platform dependency:** CWS policy + OAuth verification + DOM coupling — three Google-controlled surfaces that can shift under us.\n- **Re-review on change:** each scope addition re-triggers OAuth verification; adding a restricted scope = CASA. Calendar-only is a permanent discipline, not a one-time choice.\n\n---\n\n## Sequencing recommendation\n\n1. **Internal-first spike (no verification).** Force-install an unlisted extension to our Workspace. Build the magic-address detect + one-click \"mark visitor\" + Option A banner + side-panel UI (template preview, toggles, edits) against the existing engine endpoints. Prove the UX with real hosts.\n2. **Validate two things before committing to maintain it forever:**\n   - Are hosts actually on **desktop** when they register visitors? (If mobile-heavy, the add-on stays primary and the extension is a niche desktop add-on.)\n   - Is the UX win over the add-on card **big enough to justify the DOM-maintenance tax**?\n3. **If both hold:** extension becomes the primary **desktop** surface; add-on remains the **mobile** surface; both key off the magic address; engine nudges async via FCM/WhatsApp/Chat.\n4. **Public/commercial = packaging + verification exercise** over code that already works — same staged path the add-on follows. Don't pay verification/legal cost until the internal version has earned it.\n\n---\n\n## The unified vision (one signal, many reactors)\n\n```\n              magic address on a calendar event  ◄── the one intentional \"visitor event\" signal\n                          │\n        ┌─────────────────┼──────────────────────┐\n        ▼                 ▼                       ▼\n   Desktop:          Mobile:                 Async / offline:\n   Chrome extension  Workspace add-on        engine watch → FCM /\n   (rich UI,         (card flow,             WhatsApp / Chat nudge\n   Option A auto-    same magic address)\n   surface)\n                          │\n                          ▼\n                  office-ops-engine (OAuth holder, dedup, issuance, lifecycle)\n```\n\nThis matches the umbrella architecture: channel-agnostic core, plugin-shaped domain, dumb adapters. The **magic address — not the extension — is what unifies the vision across devices.**\n\n---\n\n## Open questions to resolve before/with the build\n\n- Which **persona** dominates host visitor-registration: desktop or mobile? (Decides whether the extension is primary or niche.)\n- Exact **magic-address form** for the extension to detect (guest email vs. location vs. resource) — must match what the engine ingest already keys on.\n- Whether the one-click banner is enough, or Option B (zero-click overlay) is needed — decide on evidence, not upfront.\n- Billing model for the eventual commercial version (per-seat / per-org / freemium) — affects the OAuth/data-processor commitments.\n"
}
```

1	# Spec — Auxilio Workspace add-on → engine (card-action endpoints)
2	
3	**Date:** 2026-06-16 (rev 2 — card-first) · **Scope:** the engine-side contract the `auxilio-workspace/` Calendar add-on calls.
4	**Plan:** `../../Planning-docs/2026-06-16_calendar_visitor_addon_build_plan.md`
5	**Code touched (all additive):** new routes in `routes.ts`; a `visit_drafts` store; a **gated** draft-aware branch in `calendar-ingest.ts`; an ID-token verifier. **No existing route, signature, or scope changes.**
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 0. Two corrections that shape this spec
10	
11	1. **The spine already exists.** `ingestCalendarEvent(NormalizedCalendarEvent)` in `calendar-ingest.ts` already dedups on `tenantId + iCalUid` via `calendar_event_links`, handles create/reschedule/cancel, and `CalendarEventSource` already includes `'marketplace'`. **Do not build `upsertVisitFromCalendarEvent`.**
12	2. **Card-first (rev 2).** The host flow lives entirely in the CardService card — no web app. So the engine exposes **several small card-action endpoints** (load draft, update field, preview, send, manage), not one `register` POST. Each card interaction = action handler → one of these endpoints → re-rendered card.
13	
14	---
15	
16	## 1. Non-breaking guarantee (read first)
17	
18	The card **routes** are strictly additive. There is **one deliberate behavior change** to the calendar pipeline (the no-auto-send decision, 2026-06-17) — called out explicitly below; it is intended, not a regression.
19	
20	| Existing flow | What it uses | Status |
21	|---|---|---|
22	| **ops-dashboard** invite create / preview / bulk | `POST /api/visitor/invite`, `POST /api/visitor/preview-invite-email`, `POST /api/visitors/bulk-invite`, `PATCH …/flow-graph` (admin-session auth) | **Unchanged.** Card adds **sibling** routes under `/api/visitor/calendar/addon/*` (ID-token auth), reusing `createVisitorInvite` / `renderPassEmail` **without signature changes**. |
23	| **Slack** invite commands / approvals | Slack-signed routes + `createVisitorInvite` | **Unchanged** — no shared signature changes. |
24	| **visitor-web** guard verify / check-in / register | `/api/visitor/verify/*`, `/visitor/register`, session routes | **Unchanged** — different surface entirely. |
25	| **Slack-OAuth calendar** (per-user poll) | `calendar-sync.ts` → `ingestCalendarEvent(..., source:'oauth')`; scope `calendar.events.readonly` (`CURRENT_SCOPE_VERSION='v2-contacts'`) | **OAuth scope unchanged** → `markStaleScopeConnections` doesn't fire → no reconnect storm. **Behavior change (intended):** the poll no longer auto-creates passes — `ingestCalendarEvent` now **builds a Visit Draft** (status `'drafted'`) for the host to send from the add-on. |
26	| **`.ics` magic-address** inbound | `/api/visitor/calendar/inbound` → `ingestCalendarEvent(..., source:'ics-email')` | Same intended change — **drafts instead of auto-creating** invites. |
27	
28	**The change to shared code** (`ingestCalendarEvent`): the new-event and never-sent-reschedule paths now call `draftFromEvent` (build/refresh a Visit Draft, **no invites**) instead of `createInvitesForEvent`. Invites are created **only** via `/addon/send` or the **draft-authoritative reschedule** (moving already-sent passes). Cancel still cancels sent passes. This is the **no-auto-send product decision** (all calendar paths, effective now) — a deliberate gap until the add-on ships.
29	
30	---
31	
32	## 2. Card-action endpoint set
33	
34	All under `/api/visitor/calendar/addon/*`, all **ID-token authed** (§3), all return JSON the card re-renders from.
35	
36	| Method · Path | Purpose | Reuses |
37	|---|---|---|
38	| `POST /addon/draft` | Load (or lazily create) the **Visit Draft** for an event. Body: `{ iCalUid, providerEventId?, attendees[], title?, start?, end? }`. Returns the curated roster + per-guest status. Hits the **pre-warmed** draft when the watch built it (§ plan §6). | `visit_drafts` store |
39	| `PATCH /addon/draft` | Persist a host edit: per-guest `include` toggle, name, phone, pass/email template; visit-level location. Body: `{ iCalUid, patch }`. Idempotent. | `visit_drafts` store |
40	| `POST /addon/preview` | Render the invite email for one guest. Body: `{ iCalUid, visitorEmail }`. Returns `{ subject, html, text }` (card shows a native summary; "send test to me" optional). | **`renderPassEmail`** (same fn the dashboard preview uses) |
41	| `POST /addon/send` | Materialize invites from the **included** draft guests, honoring overrides. Returns per-guest `{ visitorEmail, invitationId, passUrl, status }`. | **`createVisitorInvite`** + `calendar_event_links` upsert |
42	| `POST /addon/cancel-guest` | Cancel one guest's invite. Body: `{ iCalUid, invitationId }`. | existing `cancelInvitationById` |
43	
44	> Auth differs from the dashboard's admin-session routes, which is **why these are separate routes** rather than reusing `/api/visitor/invite`. The *logic* underneath is the shared functions — no duplication of business rules.
45	
46	---
47	
48	## 3. Auth — ID-token verification
49	
50	Mirror the existing `verifyIdToken` usage at `google-oauth.ts:123`. New helper `verifyAddonIdToken(bearer): Promise<{ email, name, hd }>`:
51	
52	```ts
53	const ticket = await new OAuth2Client().verifyIdToken({
54	  idToken,
55	  audience: process.env.AUXILIO_WORKSPACE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID, // accept a comma-list (web + mobile clients)
56	});
57	// require email_verified; lowercase email; read hd (hosted domain)
58	```
59	
60	- Verified **email = host/organizer**. Never trust an organizer in the body (forgery guard).
61	- **Domain gate** via the existing internal-domains notion → reject non-internal hosts (internal-first).
62	- `hd` is the future multi-tenant key; for now `tenantId` defaults to `'appointy'`.
63	- New env: `AUXILIO_WORKSPACE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` (document in `env.updated`, not committed).
64	
65	---
66	
67	## 4. Visit Draft + the gated draft-authoritative rule
68	
69	**Store:** a new `visit_drafts` table keyed on `(tenant_id, ical_uid)` — roster JSON `[{ email, name, phone, include, passTemplate, emailTemplate, status }]` + visit-level `{ location, hostEmail }` + `materialized` flag. (Alternative: extend `calendar_event_links`; a dedicated table is cleaner — open question.)
70	
71	**Pre-warm:** the `calendar-watch.ts` hook builds the draft (attendees + phone-from-history + defaults) when the event is created/changed, so `POST /addon/draft` is a warm read.
72	
73	**Send** (`/addon/send`): for each `include:true` guest → `createVisitorInvite({...overrides, invitedVia:'calendar', approvalTier:'invited'})` → collect ids → **upsert `calendar_event_links`** (so dedup/cancel/reschedule converge) with a `draft_authoritative` marker → mark the draft `materialized`.
74	
75	**The one shared-code change — gated, in `ingestCalendarEvent`:**
76	
77	```
78	on create/update for an iCalUid:
79	  if a draft_authoritative ledger row exists:        # NEW branch
80	     - cancel  → cancel the curated invites (as today)
81	     - reschedule → cancel old + reissue from the DRAFT roster at the new time
82	     - no time change → duplicate (noop)
83	     # never regenerate from raw attendees → host customization preserved
84	  else:                                              # EXISTING code, verbatim
85	     - today's createInvitesForEvent(...) path
86	```
87	
88	So passive producers (`'oauth'`, `'ics-email'`) on a **curated** event only retime/cancel; on a **non-curated** event they behave exactly as now. Convergence stays keyed on `iCalUid`.
89	
90	---
91	
92	## 5. Write-back & OAuth scope — the no-reconnect-storm decision
93	
94	**Revises plan D7.** Card-first means write-back to the open event happens **inside the Apps Script add-on**, which has the narrow **current-event** scope available:
95	
96	```
97	addOns.calendar.currentEventAccess = READ_WRITE
98	.../auth/calendar.addons.current.event.read|write
99	```
100	
101	So the add-on writes the "Reception ✓ / pass link" onto the open event itself. **We do NOT widen the shared per-user OAuth** (`calendar.events.readonly`, used by the Slack poll) to read+write, because bumping `CURRENT_SCOPE_VERSION` would flip every connected host to `reconnect_required` and stop their polling until re-consent. Broad calendar write is **not needed for v1** and is deliberately avoided.
102	
103	- Per-user OAuth connection: **unchanged** (`readonly`, same scope version).
104	- Write-back: **add-on current-event scope** (granted at add-on install, not via the Slack connection).
105	- Still calendar-only / sensitive → no CASA. Never add Gmail/Drive.
106	
107	(If we ever need background write when the event is *closed*, that's a future scope-version bump handled with a migration + reconnect prompt — explicitly out of scope now.)
108	
109	---
110	
111	## 6. Idempotency & convergence
112	- Send must use the **canonical `iCalUid`** (add-on reads it via `Calendar.Events.get(...).iCalUID`, not synthesized) so the curated invites land on the same `calendar_event_links` row as any `.ics`/OAuth copy.
113	- Order-independent: room-resource auto-creates if it arrives first (no draft); once the host curates + sends, the row becomes `draft_authoritative` and passive paths stop regenerating.
114	- Regression test: same event via `/inbound` and `/addon/send` → one invite per guest.
115	
116	---
117	
118	## 7. Build checklist (Phase 0 status — 2026-06-17)
119	- [x] `verifyAddonIdToken` + `isInternalHostEmail` helper (`addon-auth.ts`); env `AUXILIO_WORKSPACE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID`.
120	- [x] `visit_drafts` table (`postgres-schema.ts`) + `draft_authoritative` column on `calendar_event_links`.
121	- [x] `visit-drafts.ts` store (get/build/patch/materialize/markMaterialized + phone-from-history pre-fill).
122	- [x] Five `/api/visitor/calendar/addon/*` routes (§2), ID-token authed, reusing `createVisitorInvite` / `renderPassEmail` / `cancelInvitationById`.
123	- [x] Gated `draft_authoritative` branch in `ingestCalendarEvent`; ledger writer `recordDraftMaterialization` + reconcile helper `getLinkedInvitationIds` (§4).
124	- [x] Confirmed **no** change to `CURRENT_SCOPE_VERSION` or the shared OAuth scope.
125	- [x] `npm run build` green; `tsc --noEmit` clean for all new/changed files (20 errors are pre-existing project debt in untouched files).
126	- [x] **Pre-warm hook** wired in `calendar-sync.ts` (OAuth poll), **gated behind `AUXILIO_WORKSPACE_PREWARM=1` (default OFF)** so it doesn't create speculative drafts before the add-on ships. Best-effort, never affects sync. `/addon/draft` lazy-create covers correctness when the flag is off. (Note: the OAuth poll still auto-creates invites — the add-on curate-vs-auto-send interaction for OAuth-connected hosts is an unresolved product decision, see below.)
127	- [x] **Test harness** added (`bun test`, script `"test": "bun test src/mastra/modules/visitor"`). **Unit tests** (`addon-auth.test.ts`, `visit-drafts.test.ts`) run anywhere — 10 pass. **Integration tests** (`calendar-addon.integration.test.ts`: no-draft regression + `'drafted'` + draft-authoritative convergence) are **opt-in** — `RUN_ADDON_DB_TESTS=1` + a **throwaway** `DATABASE_URL` (NOT the dev/prod DB). Gating on `DATABASE_URL` presence alone was wrong — it wrote to the real DB.
128	- [x] **Verified Track A** (integration tests, 3/3) and **Track B** (HTTP end-to-end) against an **ephemeral local Postgres** (homebrew `initdb` in `/tmp`, torn down after). Track B proved over real HTTP: `.ics` inbound → `'drafted'` + **0 invites**; `/addon/draft` → roster; `PATCH` → exclude guest + set phone; `/addon/preview` → branded email; `/addon/send` → **1 invite for the included guest only**.
129	- **DEV-ONLY add-on auth bypass:** `verifyAddonIdToken` honors `ADDON_DEV_TRUST_EMAIL` (inert unless set AND `NODE_ENV !== 'production'`) so the `/addon/*` routes can be exercised before the Apps Script add-on exists. Minimal HTTP harness: `scripts/dev-visitor-http.ts` (mounts only `handleVisitorRequest`, no heavy app boot). **Never set `ADDON_DEV_TRUST_EMAIL` in prod.**
130	
131	### Resolved (decision 2026-06-17)
132	- **No auto-send — all calendar paths, effective now.** Implemented: `ingestCalendarEvent` builds Visit Drafts instead of auto-creating invites (both `'oauth'` and `'ics-email'`); the redundant flag-gated pre-warm was removed from `calendar-sync.ts`. Invites are created only on explicit `/addon/send` (or draft-authoritative reschedule). Accepted trade-off: calendar→pass is draft-only (no passes auto-issued) until the add-on UI + nudge ship — a deliberate, known gap.
133	
134	### Do NOT
135	- Build `upsertVisitFromCalendarEvent`, or change `createVisitorInvite` / `ingestCalendarEvent` signatures.
136	- Touch `/api/visitor/invite`, `/preview-invite-email`, `/bulk-invite`, or the Slack/visitor-web routes.
137	- Widen / re-version the shared calendar OAuth scope (reconnect storm).
138	- Trust `organizer` from the request body.
139	- Add Gmail/Drive scopes.
140	- Regenerate invites from raw attendees when a draft is authoritative.
